opening: “My sheep hear my voice, says the Lord; I know them, and they follow me.” — John 10:27
body:
For days, my prayers have grown longer, more frequent, and more desperate. Financial uncertainty, ongoing struggles, and the fear of what might come next have weighed heavily upon me. I have prayed with an urgency that sometimes feels inseparable from my suffering.

Yesterday, a burden was finally lifted. Money we had been waiting for arrived, and for the first time in a while, I felt I could breathe.

I was deeply grateful.

But almost immediately, I noticed something that unsettled me. With the relief of my circumstances came a lessening of the urgency I had felt in prayer.

It was subtle, but I recognized it.

Why did I seem to reach for Jesus so desperately when I was afraid, yet feel less compelled to reach for Him when that fear subsided?

I know that my love for Him had not diminished. But I also recognized how easily the comfort of improved circumstances could occupy the place where my desperate longing for Him had been.

And I didn't like that realization.

I don't want to need despair to feel close to Jesus. I don't want my deepest prayers to come only when I am frightened, or my greatest reverence to emerge only when I have nowhere else to turn.

I want to seek Him just as earnestly in thanksgiving as I do in suffering. I want the abundance of my gratitude to equal the abundance of my pleading.

For so long, I have been asking Him for relief. Yet when relief came, I realized that I had momentarily confused the easing of my circumstances with the peace I had been seeking.

I don't want my circumstances to be the source of my peace. I want Jesus to be my peace, whatever my circumstances.

And this is difficult.

When we are frightened, we pray for the strength to surrender. We tell Jesus we trust Him, but we continue searching for ways to make everything work. Sometimes we finally let go, not because surrender has become easy, but because we have exhausted everything else we know to do.

Then something changes. A door opens. A burden lifts. And we breathe again.

But what happens to that surrender when we no longer feel desperate?

Today's Gospel reminds me of the tenderness of Jesus. He stands before those who cannot answer Him, and rather than force their understanding, He demonstrates His mercy. He invites them to recognize His love without demanding their response.

Perhaps I need to recognize that same tenderness toward myself.

Jesus does not ask me to remain afraid so that I will remain close to Him. He does not need my desperation to know that I love Him.

He invites me to know Him in every circumstance.

I am learning that the depth of prayer cannot be measured by the intensity of my suffering. And perhaps true surrender is not simply reaching for Jesus when everything else has failed, but continuing to rest in Him when everything seems to be going well.

I want to bring Him my joy with the same openness as my sorrow, my thanksgiving with the same sincerity as my pleading, and my ordinary days with the same devotion as my darkest nights.

Because I do not want merely to find Jesus when I need relief. I want to find my relief in Jesus.
prayer: Lord Jesus,  You know how desperately I have sought You in my struggles, and how quickly my heart responds when those struggles begin to ease.  Teach me to love You with the same devotion in peace as in uncertainty. Let my thanksgiving be as sincere as my pleading, and my joy as prayerful as my sorrow.  Help me surrender not only what frightens me, but also the comforts and securities I am tempted to hold more closely than You.  May I never confuse the passing relief of my circumstances with the enduring peace of Your presence.  I want You in every moment, Lord—not only when I have nowhere else to turn, but especially when life gives me room to breathe.  Amen.
theme: When suffering brings us urgently to Jesus, can we learn to seek Him with that same devotion when relief finally comes?
title: THANKSGIVING
